query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex single‐phase high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges under service‐relevant conditions (elevated temperature and high strain rate) because dynamic grain refinement induces a population of high‐angle, nanocrystalline grain boundaries that lack the stabilizing effects of segregation. These boundaries have increased free energy and lower cohesive strength, leading to cavitation and intergranular decohesion during mechanical loading—a mechanism distinct from the segregation-driven embrittlement in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially coarse-grained, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled, high-temperature (e.g., 400–800°C) and high-strain rate mechanical loading (e.g., rapid tensile or sliding tests) to trigger dynamic grain refinement, while maintaining an inert or ultra-high vacuum environment to exclude chemical effects.
generation.conditions: Comparative tests between a baseline condition at room temperature/low strain rate and the intervention condition at elevated temperature/high strain rate; testing must avoid oxidation or extrinsic segregation phenomena.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanocrystalline surface or localized layer featuring high-angle grain boundaries with grain sizes approaching 10–50 nm.
generation.mechanism: High strain rates and elevated temperatures promote severe plastic deformation that dynamically refines the grain size. Once the grain size falls below a critical threshold, dislocation activity is suppressed and grain-boundary sliding becomes dominant. The resulting high-energy grain boundaries, without compensatory segregation or precipitation, are more prone to decohesion and cavitation, leading to brittle failure modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under intervention conditions, the alloy is expected to exhibit a decrease in ductility and toughness—manifested as early intergranular crack initiation and brittle fracture—compared to the ductile behavior seen in the baseline condition. Microstructural analysis should reveal a refined grain structure with evidence of grain-boundary decohesion.
generation.baseline: The same alloy under room-temperature and low strain rate loading, which shows uniform deformation and ductile fracture without significant grain refinement or intergranular decohesion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for service conditions where the alloy is exposed to high-temperature, high-strain rate loading in inert environments. Results may differ if extrinsic chemical effects or non-mechanical degradation processes are present.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative mechanism is supported by observations of grain-boundary decohesion in HEAs, the quantitative onset of brittleness (e.g., the critical grain size and the exact reduction in toughness) is uncertain due to possible competing effects like dynamic recrystallization or local amorphization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of single-phase CoCrFeMnNi alloy specimens. Divide them into two groups: Group A for high-temperature (e.g., 600°C) and high-strain rate (e.g., rapid tensile or sliding) testing in an inert or UHV environment, and Group B for baseline testing at room temperature and low strain rate. After deformation, use TEM/SEM to evaluate the grain size distribution and look for signatures of grain-boundary decohesion (e.g., cavitation or intergranular cracks). Simultaneously, perform standardized fracture toughness tests on both groups.
measurements: Fractographic analysis to distinguish intergranular versus transgranular fracture modes
Strain rate and temperature records during testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Group A does not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness, nor evidence of an increased population of nanocrystalline (10–50 nm) high-angle grain boundaries with signs of decohesion compared to Group B, then the hypothesis—that high-temperature and high-strain rate loading induces brittle behavior via dynamic grain boundary decohesion—will be falsified.

Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
